title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.

progress.text: Bulatov proves the ordinary finite-template CSP dichotomy, covering the special case \(A=B\).
Zhuk independently proves the same ordinary CSP dichotomy; the final arXiv revision is dated 2 October 2020.
Brakensiek and Guruswami give a symmetric Boolean promise-CSP dichotomy with negations; the checked revised manuscript is dated 6 May 2021.
Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz classify all symmetric Boolean promise CSPs without requiring negations.
Barto establishes a tractable finite promise pair whose every finite intermediate exact CSP is NP-complete.
Krokhin and Opršal survey the open general classification and distinguish decision from search.
The Banakh–Barsukov–Nakajima preprint proves the Promise MMSNP correspondence and states a monochromatic-clique dichotomy with conditional hardness; it subsequently appears at LICS 2026.

The published Krokhin–Vagnozzi theorem proves NP-hardness for \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) and completes the three-element symmetric ternary target classification for approximations of exactly-one satisfaction.

status_note: An open general classification question in the 2022 survey and the published July 2026 Krokhin–Vagnozzi article. The latter resolves a restricted three-element target family; the May 2026 Promise MMSNP preprint gives a logical correspondence and a conditional monochromatic-clique classification. Bounded checks through 14 September 2026 found no full unconditional finite-pair dichotomy or counterexample. Individual theorem statements and scopes were checked, but their full proofs were not independently verified.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.

sentences: A finite promise CSP distinguishes inputs satisfying stronger local constraints from inputs failing even weaker constraints.
The question asks whether every fixed finite template pair has a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm or is NP-hard under promise-preserving many-one reductions.
The algorithm or reduction may depend on the pair, and no effective procedure for classifying input templates is required.
The ordinary CSP dichotomy and several promise subclasses are known, but relaxing the constraints changes the classification problem substantially.
The checked 2026 results concern restricted families and leave this full unconditional decision dichotomy open in the cited sources.
